title: Translating business problems into Claude solutions
titleVi: Chuyển bài toán kinh doanh thành giải pháp dùng Claude

units.text: Translate business problems into Claude-based AI solutions
What you will be able to do
Map a business process step by step and find the steps where Claude adds value before choosing any technology
Decide, step by step, whether an LLM or a conventional approach fits better
Pick the simplest solution shape (a single augmented call, a workflow or an agent) that solves the problem
Match the solution shape to a build path: Claude apps, the Messages API, the Agent SDK or Managed Agents
Choose a model tier that fits each workload's volume, latency, cost and reasoning needs
Tie each success criterion to the business outcome it serves
Key concept
Process-first solution design

Start by mapping how the business does the work today and where the pain sits. Then give Claude only the steps where it clearly helps, using the simplest shape and build path that solves the problem. The model and the architecture come after the process is understood.

Map the business process before choosing a model

A business problem arrives as a complaint, not as a spec. Tickets land with the wrong team, support queues overflow during a launch, or lawyers spend hours summarising contracts. Asking "which model?" at this point skips the real question: which part of the current process causes the pain? Anthropic's ticket-routing guide opens by investigating the existing system, before any prompt is written. It asks how the support team routes tickets today, what decides the SLA a ticket gets, and whether the routing chooses a support tier or a product specialist.

The most revealing question is where the current automation breaks. If rules or workflows are already in place, find out exactly where they fail and how the team handles edge cases and ambiguous tickets. Those failure points are usually where the value sits. A keyword rule that sends every ticket mentioning "payment" to billing works until a customer writes about a payment-page bug. That ticket is a software problem, and a human fixes the routing by hand. Each manual correction like that is a cost you can count, and a step Claude might take over.

Once the process is mapped, break the target interaction into separate tasks. Customer support chat looks like one feature, but it is a collection of multiple different tasks, from question answering to information retrieval to taking action on requests. Anthropic's worked example is a car-insurance support chatbot: a customer opens a chat, asks about coverage for a new electric car, drifts into an off-topic question, then asks for a quote. Its tasks are greeting, product information, conversation management (staying on topic about car insurance) and quote generation through an API. Each task gets its own prompt and its own evaluation. You cannot test "the chatbot" as a whole, but you can test whether quote generation asks the right eligibility questions.
Apply it to your own work

Pick a process you know well, such as invoice approval, onboarding or incident triage. Which step has the most manual rework today, and would a person describe that rework as a judgement call or a lookup?
Exam trap
Treat a customer support chatbot as one task, with one prompt and one overall quality score.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 1 of 9
Check yourself

An insurer wants a Claude support chatbot that greets customers, answers questions about electric-car coverage, stays on the topic of car insurance and produces quotes through a quoting API. The team plans to write one system prompt and track one overall quality score for "the chatbot". What should they do before building?
Build it as an autonomous agent, because the chat calls an external API and covers several kinds of request
Launch with one prompt and use customer satisfaction surveys as the overall score, since that measures what the business cares about
Write the single prompt as planned, but start on the most capable model so one overall score is enough to judge quality
Split the interaction into separate tasks (greeting, product information, conversation management, quote generation) and write prompts and evaluations for each one

Decide which steps Claude should do

Not every step in the map belongs to an LLM. Claude earns a step when the work involves language, judgement or variety that rigid systems handle badly. For ticket classification, Anthropic lists concrete signals that favour Claude over traditional ML:
Labelled data is scarce: Claude can classify with a few dozen labelled examples, where traditional ML needs massive labelled datasets.
Categories change often: Claude adapts to new or redefined classes without extensive relabelling.
Inputs are unstructured, or classes are defined by conditions rather than by examples.
Decisions must be explainable: Claude can give human-readable reasons for each classification.
Tickets arrive in many languages, and you do not want a separate model for each one.

In support chat, the signals relate to volume and coverage. Claude handles a large number of similar questions efficiently, which frees human agents for complex issues. It also provides round-the-clock coverage and absorbs sudden spikes without new hires. If none of these apply, Claude may not be the right tool for the step. A stable, well-labelled, single-language classification problem that a traditional model already solves is one example.

The model's limits shape the design too. A language model produces text by predicting the next token, so every answer is the most plausible continuation, not a looked-up fact. That works well for summaries and classifications, and it fails in predictable places: a citation that reads correctly but does not exist, a precise figure or name the model never learned, anything that happened after its knowledge cutoff, and details specific to your company that were never in its training data. Where coverage is thin, the model still writes fluent text, so fabrication looks the same as accuracy. A step that needs current or company-specific facts is therefore designed with retrieval, web search or a tool from the start. Any step whose output cannot be checked needs a human or a programmatic gate after it.
On the exam

When a scenario describes the business problem, look for the answer that changes the painful step and leaves the working steps alone. Rebuilding the whole process around an LLM is rarely the intended answer.
Checkpoint 2 of 9
Check yourself

A support pipeline has three steps. First, a keyword rule routes tickets, and agents fix misrouted ambiguous tickets by hand every day. Second, a database lookup sets each ticket's SLA from the customer's contract tier. Third, a script posts the ticket to the chosen team's queue. Where should Claude go first?
Replace the SLA lookup, because Claude can reason about contract tiers more flexibly than a database query
Leave the pipeline unchanged, because routing tickets is a classification problem and traditional systems already handle classification
Replace only the keyword routing step, where ambiguous tickets are misrouted and corrected by hand, and leave the lookup and posting as they are
Rebuild the whole pipeline around Claude so one model owns routing, the SLA lookup and queue posting
Sources
Pick the simplest solution shape
Predict first
A team must summarise each incoming legal document into a fixed set of fields, using clause definitions from an internal glossary. What shape is the best starting point?
An orchestrator that hands each clause to its own worker agent
An autonomous agent that decides which tools to call and when it is finished
A single Claude call, given the relevant glossary entries and a few examples

The rule for solution shape is to use the simplest one that works, and add complexity only when evidence shows it is needed. Sometimes that means not building an agentic system at all. Agentic systems often trade latency and cost for better task performance, so every step up has to pay for itself. From simplest to most complex, there are three shapes.
The base is the
augmented LLM

: one call to a model that has retrieval, tools and memory. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is this shape with a retrieval step that adds relevant documents to the prompt. Ticket routing, for example, is a classification task. One well-prompted call that returns its reasoning and an intent label solves it.
Next come
workflows

, where LLMs and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. Your code fixes the sequence, for example classify, then hand off to a specialised prompt. This makes the system predictable and consistent for well-defined tasks.
At the top are
agents

, where the LLM directs its own process and tool use and decides how to reach the goal. Agents win when the steps cannot be known in advance and flexible, model-driven decisions are needed at scale. A coding change that touches an unknown number of files is the typical case.

The process map tells you which shape you need. If the mapped steps are fixed and the same every time, code can sequence them, so build a workflow. If the number or order of steps depends on the input, the model has to decide, so build an agent. The specific workflow patterns, such as chaining, routing and orchestrator-workers, are compared in
architectural patterns
Exam trap
A business process that touches several systems needs an autonomous agent.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 3 of 9
Match them up
Each situation below needs a solution shape. Match each shape to the situation where it is the simplest one that works.
Tap a term, then the definition that fits it.
Augmented LLM (one call with retrieval, tools or examples)
Workflow (predefined code paths)
Agent (the model directs its own process and tool use)
The same steps every time: classify the request, then pass it to a specialised prompt, with the order fixed in code
Sort each incoming support ticket into an intent category, returning a short reason and a label
Make a coding change where the number of files to edit, and what changes in each, depends on the request
Sources
Match the shape to a build path

After the shape comes the build path, and the deciding question is how much of the implementation you want to own. The three API-based paths trade control against offloaded work. The Messages API gives the most control, because you write the agent loop and run your own tools and infrastructure. The Agent SDK provides the loop and tool execution in a process you operate. Managed Agents offloads the most: Anthropic hosts the loop, tool execution and runtime.
Build paths and what each one gives you
You want to
Use
What you get
Call the Claude API directly from your own code
Client SDK (Messages API)
Direct API access; you write the tool loop yourself, or let the beta tool runner drive it
Embed an agent in your own Python or TypeScript application, in a process you operate
Agent SDK
Claude Code's built-in tools, permissions, sessions, hooks and subagents as a library
Have Anthropic host the agent, configured through the Claude API
Managed Agents
A hosted harness running the loop, with sessions in an Anthropic-managed or self-hosted sandbox
Do interactive development or run one-off tasks from a terminal
Claude Code CLI
The terminal interface, built for daily interactive use

Each shape points toward a natural build path. A single augmented call or a short workflow fits the Messages API, because many patterns take only a few lines of code there. Starting with the API directly also keeps the prompts and responses visible, so they are easier to debug than behind a framework's abstractions. An agent that needs file, shell and web tools inside your own service fits the Agent SDK. A workload that runs for minutes or hours, needs sandboxed cloud infrastructure, or should not require you to build a loop and sandbox at all fits Managed Agents. Managed Agents can also run sandboxes on your own infrastructure when compliance or data residency requires it.

Some business problems need no build at all. In the Claude apps, artifacts let a non-developer describe a tool in conversation and get a shareable interactive app without writing code. An internal team that needs a flashcard generator or a small form helper can start there. Engineering effort is better spent on the processes that need system integration.
Exam trap
Managed Agents is just the Agent SDK with a different name, so the choice between them does not matter.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 4 of 9
Match them up
Three teams have each already chosen a solution shape. Now they have to decide how much of the implementation to own. Match each build path to the team it fits best.
Tap a term, then the definition that fits it.
Messages API (Client SDK)
Agent SDK
Managed Agents
A team wants an agent with built-in file, shell and web tools embedded in its own Python service, running in a process it operates
A team needs an agent that runs for hours in a sandbox and does not want to build or operate the agent loop, tool execution or runtime
A team building a short classify-then-hand-off workflow wants to write the tool loop in its own code and see every prompt and response while debugging

Fit the model tier to each workload
Model choice comes last because it depends on what the mapped steps demand: capability, speed and cost.
Model selection trade-offs
covers this in depth. At the solution-design level, match each workload's profile to the tier built for it.
Workload profile against the model tier to start with
When you need
Start with
Example workloads
The lowest latency and price
Claude Haiku 5.5
Real-time applications, high-volume intelligent processing, cost-sensitive deployments needing strong reasoning, sub-agent tasks
Speed and capability for everyday coding, agent and enterprise workloads
Claude Sonnet 5.5
Code generation, data analysis, content creation, visual understanding, agentic tool use
Complex agentic coding and enterprise work
Claude Opus 5.5
Multihour autonomous coding agents, large-scale refactoring, complex systems engineering, computer use
The highest available capability
Claude Fable 5.1
Agent sessions that run for hours, multistep deep research, analysis carried through to a finished document
Read the requirements in a scenario as a profile and match it to a tier. Here are three common profiles:
Haiku: high volume, tight latency, tight cost.

Take a chat widget that must answer within a few hundred milliseconds at flash-sale volume, on a strict per-conversation budget. That profile points to Haiku. Haiku is still built for deployments needing strong reasoning, so multi-turn troubleshooting does not by itself push the workload up a tier. Ticket routing is the same profile: Haiku is the fastest and most cost-effective current model and handles high-volume classification well.
Opus: multi-hour autonomous work, correctness over cost.

An agent that plans and runs a multi-hour refactor of a large legacy codebase, with few human checkpoints, fits Opus. Opus is built for long-running agentic coding and large-scale refactoring. Running many cheap parallel attempts or adding context does not make up for weaker reasoning on that work.
Sonnet: one default for everyday work.

A company-wide default for code generation, data analysis, drafting and agentic tool use fits Sonnet. Sonnet balances speed and capability for everyday workloads without premium pricing on every call.

Effort is a setting, supported by several Claude models, that trades intelligence (how much reasoning the model applies) against latency and cost within a single model. Turning it down makes responses faster and cheaper, and turning it up buys more reasoning on hard problems, so tuning it is often a better lever than switching models.

For a new build, there are two ways to start testing. The cost-first path begins with Haiku, tests the use case thoroughly, and upgrades only to close a specific capability gap. The capability-first path begins with Opus for complex reasoning or high-autonomy agentic work, then lowers effort or moves to a smaller model as the workflow is optimised. The process map often uses both. A cheap tier handles bulk steps such as routing, and a stronger tier handles the few hard ones.
Exam trap
Any workload that involves multi-turn reasoning needs Sonnet or Opus, even under tight latency and cost limits.
Why is that wrong?
Checkpoint 5 of 9
Check yourself

During a flash sale, a retailer's support widget has to reply within a few hundred milliseconds. It handles thousands of conversations at once on a strict per-conversation budget. Some conversations involve multi-turn troubleshooting. Which model should the team start testing with?
Claude Sonnet 5.5, because any conversational workload with reasoning needs at least the middle tier
Claude Haiku 5.5: test the use case thoroughly and upgrade only if a specific capability gap shows up
Claude Fable 5.1 with lower effort, so the most capable model gets cheap enough for high-volume chat
Claude Opus 5.5, because multi-turn troubleshooting needs deep reasoning, so the latency and budget limits have to give way
Checkpoint 6 of 9
Exam question

A retail company is building a customer-support chat widget that must handle very high message volume during flash sales, respond within a few hundred milliseconds, and stay within a tight per-conversation cost budget, while still handling multi-turn troubleshooting reasoning correctly. Which model should the architecture team select as the primary model for this workload?
Deploy Claude Opus 4.8, since its deeper reasoning guarantees troubleshooting accuracy in every conversation despite its higher per-token cost.
Deploy Claude Haiku 4.5, since it delivers near-frontier reasoning at the lowest per-token cost with the fastest response times available.
Deploy Claude Sonnet 5, since its balance of speed and intelligence justifies the extra cost for troubleshooting at flash-sale volume.
Deploy Claude Fable 5, since its very large context window lets it track every shopper's full history across simultaneous conversations.
Checkpoint 7 of 9
Exam question

An enterprise engineering organization needs an agent that can autonomously plan and execute a multi-hour refactor across a large, complex legacy codebase with minimal human checkpoints, prioritizing correctness over cost. Which model is the best fit for this workload?
Claude Haiku 4.5, because its low cost lets the team run many parallel refactor attempts within the same budget as one long session.
Claude Sonnet 5, because its speed keeps a multi-hour agent loop responsive while still handling most agentic coding tasks well.
Claude Opus 4.8, because it is built for complex agentic coding and large-scale refactoring with minimal supervision at enterprise scale.
Claude Haiku 4.5 paired with a longer context window, because extending context compensates for its lower reasoning depth on refactors.
Checkpoint 8 of 9
Exam question

A company wants a single default model for most of its internal tooling: code generation, data analysis, content drafting, and agentic tool use across many teams, seeking the best combination of frontier intelligence and everyday speed without paying premium enterprise pricing. Which model should they standardize on?
Claude Opus 4.8, because its premium reasoning is worth paying for on every team's day-to-day coding and content tasks.
Claude Sonnet 5, because it offers frontier intelligence at scale for coding, agents, and everyday workflows at moderate cost.
Claude Haiku 4.5, because its low price outweighs any reasoning gap for teams doing content drafting and data analysis.
Claude Fable 5, because its long-running agent design fits every team's mix of coding, drafting, and analysis tasks.
Sources
Tie success criteria to the business outcome

A solution is judged by whether it relieves the pain found in the process map, not by how well the model behaves in isolation. Good criteria are specific, measurable, achievable and relevant, as taught in
measurable success criteria
. The relevance part matters most here: each criterion has to trace back to a business outcome that someone in the organisation already tracks.

The support guides keep two lists apart. Task criteria cover the model's work, such as intent-comprehension accuracy of 95% or higher, or 100% accuracy on generated quotes. Business-impact criteria cover the outcome the business pays for. For a support chatbot, that means a deflection rate of typically 70–80% of inquiries handled without a human, a CSAT of 4 out of 5 or higher, and a lower average handling time than human agents. For ticket routing, the business measures include a 10–20% improvement in tickets resolved per agent, an escalation rate below 20%, and a 10–15% reduction in cost per ticket.

Each task metric should explain how it moves a business metric. If it cannot, it is a vanity metric. Routing accuracy matters because misrouted tickets get escalated and handled twice. So report routing accuracy next to the escalation rate and cost per ticket it is meant to reduce. Define both lists with the support team that owns the process, not only with the engineers building the solution. That way the targets reflect the real shape of the work, including the edge cases the team already handles by hand.
A pilot reports 97% classification accuracy, but cost per ticket has not moved. What does the process map suggest to check first?
Checkpoint 9 of 9
Check yourself
Engineers want to judge a new Claude ticket-routing step on a single number: 95% routing accuracy on a held-out test set. Which change best ties the success criteria to the business outcome?
Add classification consistency and response latency, with all three measured by the engineering team on the test set
Raise the accuracy target to 99%, because higher model accuracy is what the business is paying for
Report routing accuracy next to the escalation rate and cost per ticket it should reduce, with targets agreed with the support team that owns routing
Drop accuracy and track only CSAT, because the customer's view is the only outcome that counts
